Let 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}].$
Which of the following statements are true? 

I. $det(A)=0$

II. The lines $2x+4y=0$ and $3x+6y=0$ intersect at exactly one point

III. ${A}^{-1}$ does **not** exist

Recall that given $A=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{aligned}]$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

1\. $A$ is invertible.

2\. The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

3\. The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

4\. The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

5\. $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

- Statement I is true. We have 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =2\cdot 6-4\cdot 3 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem is false, all the other parts of the theorem are false too. Therefore, according to the theorem: 

- Statement II is false by the fourth part of the invertible matrix theorem.

- Statement III is true by the first part of the invertible matrix theorem.

Therefore, only statements I and III are true.
